data.title: Jon Stewart flames Chuck Schumer; Dems must get ready to govern
data.description:
John Stewart has a plan for the Dems when they re-take office in January.  

“Job one of this opportunity is to tear down the obstacles and old way of thinking that got us into this mess,” Said the “Daily Show” comedian. “Someone has to meet this moment and they have got to show — and this moment is not, ‘oh, we get to impeach everybody’ … like, you have an opportunity to actually govern.”  

Democrats just secured some major political victories. But winning an election and keeping the trust of voters are two very different things. Democrats would be making a mistake if they assumed this victory automatically validates the congressional leadership that got them here. It does not.  

On his podcast, “The Weekly Show,” Stewart went a step further, taking aim at Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer:  

“By the way, they’re already like, ‘Chuck Schumer deserves a lot of credit’ … Chuck Schumer fought tooth and nail against half of these [BLEEP] people! And even if he didn’t, he does not understand the urgency of the moment and what the future demands. I truly believe that.”  

He went on to say that many senior leaders need to go, and folks should remember Schumer was the genius that brought us Haley Stevens. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, was the genius who previously co-sponsored Medicare for All legislation and then went on national TV and said he’s changed his mind.  

Schumer and Jeffries were also congratulated by AIPAC on their wins this week. 

“AIPAC congratulates the hundreds of pro-Israel Democrats and Republicans who won their elections last night. More than 234 candidates supported by AIPAC members have already won, with many additional races still too close to call. We congratulate Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries on the resounding victories for their caucuses.”  

Meanwhile, both Schumer and Jeffries have faced criticism from progressives over their relationship with AIPAC and their reluctance to embrace candidates like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and others.  

The political landscape surrounding AIPAC is changing. Even Republicans are questioning our countries ties to Israel. The group and affiliated organizations spent nearly $30 million backing Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, an enormous investment that ultimately did not prevent progressive challenger Abdul El-Sayed from winning the nomination. Then the group poured money into Mike Rogers campaign. El-Sayed still won the entire election.  

But I digress. Democrats need to be careful — they cannot spend the next two years proving they are better at fighting Republicans than they are at improving people’s lives.  

Yes, there should be accountability, investigations and credible abuses of power should be examined. For example, Democrats should investigate the reported interference with Ukraine’s access to Musk’s Starlink and Starshield systems, as well as the financial relationships surrounding President Trump’s family crypto ventures, including Binance’s role in facilitating his family’s stablecoin and Trump’s subsequent pardon of the Binance founder.  

But hear me clearly: making impeachment the centerpiece of the new majority’s agenda would be a mistake.  

I say that as someone deeply critical of Trump and his administration. Do not let governing fall to the wayside. People are seriously struggling out here. A recent AP Voter Poll found that 79 percent of voters said inflation had caused their households either moderate or severe financial hardship. That’s the reality Democrats need to confront. Groceries, housing, health care, utilities. These are not abstract political talking points. This is serious.  

Schumer does not automatically have to become Senate majority leader, and Jeffries does not automatically have to become Speaker of the House. Those positions require support from their respective caucuses. Neither of them have an entitlement to the job.  

This could be an opportunity to look beyond the familiar names and find new leaders, with fewer big-pocket donors, who are willing to speak to working families, connect with younger voters, challenge entrenched political interests and offer something more compelling than simply being the alternative to Donald Trump.   

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

data.title: DC official urges incoming Democratic governors to withdraw National Guard
data.description:
Washington, D.C., officials are calling on incoming Democratic governors in five states that flipped blue to recall their National Guard troops from the nation’s capital, a move that could see some 628 guardsmen pulled from city streets come January.

During a D.C. Council hearing on Thursday, councilmember Brook Pinto (D) — the chair of the public safety committee — said she would soon send a letter on behalf of the council to ask the governors-elect in Iowa, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio and Texas to “immediately” withdraw their soldiers back to their states.

“It’s something they can do their first day in office,” she said.

“While we have asked all of the governors across the country in the past to pull back their troops, we’ve been met with a lot of resistance and a lot of governors who are following the lead from President Trump,” Pinto noted. “But we now have the opportunity, with Tuesday’s election results, to turn the tide of what we’re seeing in Washington, D.C., and to have some real accountability to the federal government.”

Some 3,100 National Guard troops are deployed in Washington as part of President Trump’s “Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful” mission, announced last summer.

Of that number, just under 760 troops are part of the D.C. National Guard — which is controlled by the sitting president — and 2,341 have been sent to the city by states and territories nearly all currently controlled by Republican governors, according to the Joint Task Force.

While Texas, Ohio and Nevada currently only have one or two guard troops sent from each of their states, Georgia and Iowa can make a far bigger dent if they pull their 514 and 110 troops, respectively.

Should Alaska also flip to a Democratic governor — the race has yet to be called but has former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) currently leading — that would be an additional 34 guardsmen who could be recalled.

Guard troops have been a common sight patrolling the streets of D.C. as part of their deployment ,which began in August 2025 when the federal government ⁠temporarily took ​over the city’s law ​enforcement through ‌presidential executive order. The number of guard members has fluctuated in the course of a year, swelling to roughly 5,000 ahead of the Fourth of July.

That presence has worried local officials and residents, with Pinto saying Thursday that congressional leaders have been “unsympathetic to what we’ve been dealing with and, in some cases, directly hostile.”

“But after Tuesday night, the tide is turning,” she said.

Pinto also condemned a directive from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth late last month, which authorized the National Guard to begin using boats, up to 60 marked police cars, and military tactical vehicles in D.C.

The action, which is sure to escalate the troops’ presence in the city and make it harder to discern between military members and law enforcement, is going in the “opposite direction” from what the city needs, she said.

Pinto also pressed the incoming Congressional Democratic majority to more rigorously conduct oversight of federal policing activity in Washington, suggesting federal agents wear identifying badges and body cameras, and ban face coverings.

data.title: Bannon says Susie Wiles should be 'removed immediately'
data.description:
Former White House adviser Steve Bannon said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and other political consultants should be “removed immediately” following the losses suffered by the GOP in the midterm elections.

Democrats secured wins in battleground states across the country on Tuesday, flipping GOP-held seats in Texas, South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Ohio, among others.

“I think that you have to look to people like Susie Wiles, the chief of staff, and the political consultants that are there … because of the results, they should be removed and removed immediately,” Bannon said in an interview with British journalist Steven Edginton.

Bannon is not the first to call for Wiles’s removal.

On Wednesday, Caroline Sunshine, a former staffer to President Trump, told Fox News that Wiles “needs to resign” and “offer her resignation to the president before he has to ask for it. Her campaign skills have not translated into governing.”

Bannon, in his interview, also raised concerns over Texas turning blue in the midterm elections.

In the Lone Star State, where Republicans have historically maintained a stronghold for years, Democratic candidates emerged victorious in key races. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated incumbent GOP Gov. Greg Abbott to be elected as the state’s first Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1994.

Democrat James Talarico also defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) to become the first Democratic senator from the state since 1988.

“Right now, in Texas we have a fight,” Bannon said, adding that the new governor, “can make Texas a sanctuary state.”

“If Texas is a sanctuary state like New York and California, you’re seeing the end of this republic as you know it,” he added.

Talarico, in a recent interview with Forbes, said he is willing to work with the Trump administration on immigration.

“I think there is an opportunity here to finally pass comprehensive immigration reform, to secure our border,” he said. “And also create more legal pathways for hard-working immigrants to come to this country, contribute to this economy and make us richer and stronger as a nation.”

data.title: Why isn't the PEACE Act law already?
data.description:
Ukraine is facing an urgent existential crisis on two inter-related fronts. Militarily, Russia has promised another brutal winter of warfare and daily war crimes without remorse for needless civilian casualties. Financially, despite massive assistance from its allies since 2022, Ukraine faces an estimated $35 billion budget gap as a direct result of Russia’s relentless illegal aggression in Europe.

With President Trump’s appeasement of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin failing to bring Russia into serious peace negotiations, Congress needs to step up its game when it reconvenes and answer a perplexing question that directly addresses Ukraine’s dual threats: Why isn’t the pending PEACE Act of 2025 law already?

The bipartisan bill would help Ukraine meet its existential crisis by mandating the accelerated transfer and repurposing of all frozen Russian funds within U.S. jurisdiction to aid Ukraine and allow it to buy defensive weapons to better protect its citizens and defend civilian infrastructure such as its vital energy grid. No U.S. taxpayer funds would be required.

The PEACE Act passed the House Financial Services Committee in July 2025 by an overwhelming 53-1 vote under the leadership of Chairman French Hill (R-Ark.) with the full support of Ranking Member Maxine Waters (D-Calif.).

This strong 53-1 committee vote projects a veto-proof majority vote in the House of Representatives if a vote is scheduled during the lame-duck session. The bill could have easily passed already on the House’s suspension calendar — an expedited voting procedure requiring a two-thirds vote, no amendments, and limited debate.

Given Ukraine’s dire financial and military predicaments, we need an answer to the question of why hasn’t this wildly popular legislation already been enacted into law?

The reason the PEACE Act is not law is the Trump administration’s failure to use these Russian assets to negotiate a desperately needed peace from a position of real strength, not cowardly weakness. It is also a result of the House Republican leadership’s abject failure to act as a co-equal branch of the U.S. government under our Constitution and schedule a vote on this noncontroversial, bipartisan legislation.

Trump’s perpetual excuse has been that he is in the middle of peace negotiations with war criminal Putin. But those negotiations have already failed and, unfortunately, peace is nowhere in sight at this moment.

A related question is how much in frozen Russian sovereign assets is subject to U.S. jurisdiction that could be transferred to Ukraine under the PEACE Act?

In 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department reported to Congress that an estimated $5 billion in Russian central bank reserves are at the Federal Reserve. However, the total amount of all additional frozen funds sitting in American correspondent banks was classified by Treasury without explanation.

While the total amount still remains a public mystery, credible experts estimate the total amount of Russian funds here range from $19 billion to as much as $50 billion out of an estimated $300 billion immobilized globally in 2022. Just think about how that money could help Ukraine if it could close its budget gap and buy U.S.-made Patriot missile defense systems to better protect its citizens and defend its sovereign territory.

Speaking on the House floor during debate on June 4 on a bipartisan Russian sanctions bill the administration opposed, Hill publicly called for House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to schedule a vote. The Speaker still has not done so. Hill then attempted to add the PEACE Act as a bipartisan amendment to this year’s National Defense Authorization Act, but his continuing efforts were ignored twice by the House Rules Committee and, by extension, House Republican leadership.

Last year’s powerful 53-1 committee vote is indicative of a veto-proof House vote and subsequent Senate vote, but only if the Speaker schedules an immediate floor vote over White House illusive objections in light of Ukraine’s immediate plight.

Once enacted, the PEACE Act would not only materially assist Ukraine but also strike a decisive financial blow to Russia’s imperialism and hybrid warfare in the rest of Europe. Russia now is a belligerent on the side of Iran and thus partially responsible for U.S. Armed Forces casualties and destruction of our forward bases and military equipment in the Middle East war. Passing this bill before Congress adjourns for the year would be an overdue signal to our allies and warning to our adversaries.

Congress must reclaim and reassert its constitutional role as a separate and coequal branch of government. It must act now to punish Russia and help Ukraine meet its dual existential threats before the onslaught of another winter of senseless warfare and reprehensible war crimes.

The PEACE Act should already be law by now.

Gregory P. Wilson was a former deputy assistant secretary of the U.S. Department of the Treasury from 1986 to 1989.

data.title: Comer says 'there's a lot of questions about Hegseth' amid impeachment push
data.description:
Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), the chair of the powerful House Oversight Committee, said on Friday that “there’s a lot of questions” in the Republican conference about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) prepares for an impeachment push next week. 

“Well, that’s going to be a decision that President Trump’s going to have to make,” Comer said during his appearance on The Hill’s sister network NewsNation when asked if he wants a new face in the Pentagon. 

“But I can tell you with a high level of confidence that there there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth. We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.” 

Comer’s comments come as The Hill reported that Trump has been asking allies about Hegseth’s standing, and one of the sources said the Pentagon chief is in “a lot of trouble.” 

Publicly, Trump has defended Hegseth, saying he was not considering replacing the Defense secretary and that Hegseth, a former Army National Guard major, is  “doing a very good job.” 

A senior Pentagon official told The Hill on Thursday the prospect of Hegseth being replaced is not “practical,” noting the difficulty of finding a replacement who could be confirmed by the Senate during the lame-duck session — and before Democrats take control of the House following the midterm blue-wave tsunami.  

“He is not terribly worried about being replaced,” the senior Pentagon official said.

Hegseth is also expected to face an impeachment salvo in the lame-duck from Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who said he would reintroduce articles of impeachment against the Pentagon chief. 

The Defense secretary ripped the impeachment push as nothing more than political theater from a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.” 

“Just like they tried against President Trump twice. You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said in a video posted on Thursday. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that,”

Massie, a vocal critic of the Iran war, has said he would not reintroduce the resolution, which is expected to have significant support from Democrats and some Republicans, if Hegseth resigns. 

Comer also said on Friday that he has heard from Republican voters who are “mad” about the Iran war, which has dragged on for over eight months, and are dissatisfied with the rise in gas prices. 

“They are mad that we’re in this situation in Iran,” Comer told NewsNation host Markie Martin. “They’re mad over gas prices, and a lot of them stayed home. I do not think, at least in Kentucky, I don’t think that these upset MAGA people voted Democrat. They just didn’t vote. So we’ve got to regain their trust. I think we can do it.”

data.title: AI companies' deceptive election ads show why Congress must scrutinize super PACs
data.description:
In many of the hottest races in this year’s midterm elections, data centers and artificial intelligence companies were effectively on the ballot. The AI industry knew how unpopular they have become, with voters across the political spectrum furious at them. So, how then could an unpopular industry pour more than $69 million into campaign ads to boost AI-friendly politicians without having their ads backfire when angry voters find out who’s behind them? Simple: Hide who really paid for the ads behind fake names.  

This was perfectly legal — and perfectly outrageous. 

Following in the footsteps of a slew of other unpopular corporate interests and billionaires before them who knew their names were toxic with voters, the AI industry’s super PAC ads hid their sponsorship behind generically named shell groups like “Defending Our Values,” “Think Big,” “American Mission,” and “Jobs and Democracy.” Almost none of the AI industry’s super PAC ads mentioned data centers or AI at all.

This is not something that favored one side or another; it’s a bipartisan problem. An AI super PAC ad for a Republican candidate featured the phrase “CHAMPION AMERICAN INNOVATION” as he shook hands with firefighters, with no mention of data centers or AI. Another AI super PAC ad for a Democrat running for a House seat praised the candidate as committed to reducing gun violence and supporting law enforcement — no mention of AI. The ads were labeled as paid for by a generically named group, not “paid for by AI companies.”

Voters deserve to know who’s really paying for the ads they see so they can make informed decisions at the ballot box. Access to actionable information is at the heart of a healthy democracy — and the very essence of what the First Amendment was designed to protect. 

Congress must close this deceptive super PAC ad loophole before the 2028 elections. The good news is that a recently introduced bill would do exactly that. Inspired by successful voter-approved campaign disclosure laws in Alaska, Arizona and California that passed with cross-partisan support, the Sunlight on SuperPACs Act recently introduced by Reps. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) and Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.) would enact a simple labeling law requiring all super PAC-funded campaign ads to include the names of their top three donors and how much they donated.  

In the case of the AI-funded super PAC ads, they could still use their shell committees to pay for them, but they would have to let voters know that the top funders of the shell committees are AI companies, executives or billionaires. That would give voters the real-time information they need to be able to evaluate the credibility of the ads by seeing who’s paying for them when they’re seeing the ads. Voters are smart but can’t make informed decisions without information.

Courts have already heard multiple corporate-funded challenges to similar state disclosure laws and upheld them all. While we strongly believe that the Supreme Court in Citizens United v. FEC was deeply mistaken in concluding that the First Amendment required allowing corporations to spend unlimited sums to influence elections, the court did unequivocally affirm the constitutionality of campaign disclosure laws.

The Supreme Court has long recognized as consistent with the First Amendment the people’s “informational interest” in requiring election campaigns to provide voters with information about the funders of election ads. Because donor transparency “enables the electorate to make informed decisions and give proper weight to different speakers and messages,” the court has consistently upheld disclosure laws. We are confident it would uphold a super PAC funders labeling law too.

Putting a true source funding label at the bottom of super PAC ads would not address the obscene amount of money being spent on American politics today or limit the questionable claims corporations and billionaires make in their campaign ads. But the Sunlight on SuperPACs Actwill empower voters to be informed about who’s behind the ads they see. Then voters can evaluate the merits of the ads for themselves. We urge the next Congress to give voters that information and shine sunlight on super PACs.

Jon Golinger is the democracy advocate for Public Citizen. Michael Beckel is Money in Politics Reform director for Issue One.

data.title: 'A Republican will never sniff the White House again' if Texas stays blue: Jesse Watters
data.description:
Fox News anchor Jesse Watters warned that if Republicans cannot return to power in Texas, the GOP may never win the presidency again. 

Watters said during his show on Thursday night that Democrats’ sweeping win in the midterm elections could be a death knell for Republicans’ chances of winning future presidential elections.

Democrats won all statewide elections on the ballot Tuesday, leaving Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) as the only remaining GOP statewide official in the Lone Star state. 

“They seize Texas and are on pace for the biggest midterm landslide since Watergate,” Watters said. “Now, if Texas stays blue, a Republican will never sniff the White House ever again.”

The Fox News personality said Republicans had two years to target Democratic opponents without many clear successes, warning that Democrats won’t “take it easy” on the GOP.

“They want it extinguished. They’re already talking about abolishing the Electoral College, impeaching the president, and executing Elon Musk. Democrat governors now control a majority of states where most of the population lives,” Watters added. 

No Democratic elected official has called for the execution of Musk.

Watters said Democrats’ near-win among White voters this cycle reinforced the Republican struggle. After showing a video of a Texas Democratic lawmaker talking about minority races joining to form a majority voting bloc in America, Watters said after Tuesday — that could work. 

“They’re talking about uniting the minority races against whites. Texas Democrat politicians are declaring a political race war. And they could win, because Republicans nearly lost the white vote Tuesday,” he said. 

“Democrats are on the cusp of winning a majority of whites, Blacks, and Hispanics. Open borders is suicide. The Democrats are about to win a Senate seat in Mississippi. Black guy. That’s like Republicans winning Hawaii,” Watters continued. 

The Fox News host said “a lot” of the blame for the midterm losses can also be pinned on the candidates, specifically Ken Paxton (R-Texas) and Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.). He said the GOP’s loss on Tuesday was not a standard midterm correction. 

“This wasn’t your standard midterm thumping,” Watters said. “When Obama got blown out in 2010 and 2014, those races were close. And he didn’t almost lose the Black vote like Republicans almost lost the White vote.”

data.title: Andrews says she won't be focused on 'retribution tour'
data.description:
South Carolina’s newly elected senator, Annie Andrews (D), said her focus will be on “delivering results” and not a “retribution tour” following her victory in the midterm elections.

In the historically red state of South Carolina, Andrews won a competitive Senate race against Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), who was picked to succeed her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

Andrews won by more than 4 percentage points and more tahn 90,000 votes, according to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill. The forecaster narrowly favored Darline Graham ahead of the elections.

“Fighting the administration is not going to lower gas prices and grocery prices. It’s not going to solve the problems that I heard about for the past eighteen months,” Andrews told Fox News during an interview. “So I’m going to be laser-focused on delivering results and not, you know, a retribution tour, because that’s what the people of South Carolina are expecting from me.”

Andrews also said she is willing to work with President Trump “to secure the border, to stop these Medicaid cuts” and to “find a way out of this war.”

“I’m going to walk up to the halls of Congress and do my best to solve as many problems as I can for the people of South Carolina,” she added.

Andrews, a pediatrician, launched her bid to run for a seat in the U.S. Senate last year. She previously ran for office in 2022 against Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), losing by around 14 points. Four years later, she won her Senate bid, becoming the first Democrat to hold a Senate seat from the state in decades.

Andrews’s win is consistent with the Democrats’ nationwide victory in the midterm elections this November, where the party took control of both the Senate and the House. Democrats secured big wins in battleground states, flipping GOP-held seats in places like Texas, Maine, Iowa, Ohio and Michigan.

data.title: Democrats can't heal the US-Canada bond Trump destroyed
data.description:
Democrats won control of both the Senate and House on Tuesday, and Canadians breathed a sigh of relief. After nearly two years of insults, economic coercion, talk of Canada becoming the 51st state, and the whole “Lake America” debacle, their relief is understandable. 

But it would be a mistake to think that Canadians are willing to return to the status quo ante — to the pre-Trump Canada-U.S. relationship. Neither this congressional election nor a change of president in 2028 is likely to restore the bilateral relationship both countries until recently considered normal. 

The international order that gave rise to that relationship is dying. It took shape and flourished within a system structured around American power: first during the Cold War’s bipolar confrontation, then during the unipolar era following the Soviet Union’s collapse. In both periods, U.S. leadership underpinned unusually close economic, political and security ties. 

For Canada, the benefits were substantial. During the Cold War, American strategic power helped secure Canada against the Soviet threat, while Ottawa and Washington developed an increasingly integrated system of continental defense.

After 1991, American dominance allowed Canada to scale back defense spending and helped sustain an open international economy in which it prospered through continental trade and multilateral cooperation. That security and prosperity also created space for Ottawa to punch above its weight as a constructive middle power. 

The arrangement was never free of friction, but its underlying logic was clear: Close integration with the U.S. made economic and strategic sense. Ironically, by enabling Ottawa to play an outsized role as a helpful fixer and respected peacekeeper, that integration also allowed Canada to be more distinctively Canadian. 

Today, that order is giving way to a more fragmented multipolar world, characterized by renewed great-power competition and the erosion of the architecture of international cooperation. Prime Minister Mark Carney captured this shift at Davos in January when he declared that “the old order is not coming back.”

His point was not simply that Canada could no longer count on an America governed by Trump. The foundations of Canadian foreign, economic and security policy were undergoing an epochal transformation.

Multipolarity complicates Canada’s traditional calculation because it changes the incentive structure in Washington. Confronted by China’s rising power, Russia’s challenge to European security and the erosion of American primacy, the U.S. is reevaluating global commitments, pressing allies to shoulder more burdens, onshoring industrial capacity and treating trade and technology as instruments of strategic competition. 

Where Washington once had greater latitude to sustain an open economy and tolerate differences with allies, it now increasingly judges close partnerships by their contribution to strategic priorities. For Canada, dependence on American power consequently carries risks that were less pronounced in the past. 

Trump has pursued this adjustment in an especially undiplomatic and confrontational fashion. His tariffs and threats against Canada have made the risks of dependence painfully clear. Yet the broader American shift toward strategic competition, economic nationalism and selective international engagement is not simply a product of Trump’s preferences. It reflects structural realities that will persist long after he leaves office. 

That is why Tuesday’s election, whatever relief it brings, will not derail or even significantly delay Canada’s ongoing strategic realignment. Congress can challenge tariffs and encourage a more cooperative bilateral relationship. A post-Trump White House may restore a measure of civility and predictability. And all of that will matter. But neither Democrats nor Republicans can recreate the international order that once made Canadian-American economic integration and strategic alignment seem both natural and optimal. 

For Ottawa, the logical response is greater strategic autonomy — not separation from the United States, but the capacity to make more choices without being unduly constrained by Washington. 

Geography and history make total rupture unrealistic. The two countries share deeply integrated supply chains, vital infrastructure and a continent whose defense requires close cooperation. Russian and Chinese capabilities, the strategic importance of the Arctic and the intensification of gray-zone competition make that cooperation more necessary, not less. The American market will likewise remain indispensable to Canadian prosperity. 

Strategic autonomy must operate within those constraints. The objective is not some sort of fortress Canada or a profound rupture of the Canada-U.S. relationship. Rather, in keeping with Prime Minister Carney’s strategy of “value-based realism,” the goal is to diversify trade where practical, strengthen Canadian defense-industrial capacity, build sovereign capabilities and enhance partnerships in Europe and the Indo-Pacific. These are means of increasing Ottawa’s freedom of action.  

Tuesday’s election may make the Canada-U.S. relationship less contentious, but it cannot reverse the overall trajectory of that relationship. Canada and the U.S. are both adapting to the emergence of a new geopolitical ecosystem — one which is generating new interests, incentives and anxieties in both capitals. 

For Ottawa, greater strategic autonomy was never merely a response to Trump. It is a rational adaptation to this new ecosystem. Whoever governs in Washington, that reality is not going away. 

Andrew Latham is a professor of international relations at Macalester College in Saint Paul, Minn., a senior fellow at the Institute for Peace and Diplomacy, and a non-resident fellow at Defense Priorities in Washington.

data.title: Waters launches bid for House Financial Services chair
data.description:
Democratic Rep. Maxine Waters (Calif.) officially launched her bid for chair of the House Financial Services Committee on Friday, after Democrats won control of the lower chamber in the midterms. 

In a letter to her Democratic colleagues, Waters — the committee’s ranking member — wrote that party lawmakers “must now deliver on our promises to the American people” and lower the cost of living. Democrats on the campaign trail vowed to ease prices, as gas and grocery costs have risen this year amid the Iran war. 

Referencing the “affordability crisis” facing Americans, the California lawmaker blasted the Trump administration for “dismantling consumer safeguards, eliminating access to safe and affordable housing” and engaging in what she described as “unprecedented levels of corruption.”

Given that, Waters wrote it “has never been more important to have a proven, effective and innovative leader” at the helm of the Financial Services panel.

“I am that leader,” she argued in her letter, which a Waters spokesperson shared with The Hill. 

Waters, 88, chaired the committee from 2019 to 2023, when Democrats last controlled the House. She has led Democrats on the panel since 2013. 

Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), who has helmed the committee since January 2025, narrowly won his reelection bid over Democrat Chris Jones.

Waters is not the only Democrat vying for the Financial Services gavel. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) launched his bid for chair on Thursday, writing in a letter to his Democratic colleagues the panel must address homeownership, frauds and scams and President Trump’s approach to white-collar crime, among other issues. 

Waters also laid out her planned agenda on Friday. The California Democrat vowed to pursue a “bold agenda,” writing she will build on the bipartisan housing law that took effect over the summer, crack down on junk fees and “permanently and independently fund” the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

The Trump administration has sought to dismantle the agency, which is an independent entity within the Federal Reserve.

As for the cryptocurrency industry, Water wrote she will “stop” the Trump family’s “crypto corruption” while establishing “tough but fair rules of the raid for legitimate crypto ventures.”

The California Democrat later proposed tweaking logistical elements of the panel, including by renaming it the “Committee on Housing and Financial Services” to put “housing first.”

She also said she will discuss “ways to empower Subcommittee chairs” with her colleagues and create three new positions: a committee whip role occupied by a junior member, a freshman representative and a committee messenger.
